title: Assess an analytics platform
prompt: A SQL team must maintain a curated star schema with T-SQL writes and multi-table transactions. A separate engineering team must preserve original PDF invoices and parse them with Spark. They want one Fabric storage foundation. Which design best satisfies all constraints?

options.text: Put PDFs in Warehouse tables and use its SQL endpoint as the Spark file store.
options.why: A relational table is not the raw-artifact storage and Spark engineering surface required here.

options.text: Keep PDFs in Lakehouse Files, process with Spark, and load curated relational data into Warehouse; both use OneLake.
options.why: This separates raw engineering from SQL-owned relational processing while sharing the storage foundation.

options.text: Keep everything in Lakehouse and perform all multi-table T-SQL writes through its SQL analytics endpoint.
options.why: That endpoint can query underlying Delta data but cannot perform those table write operations.

options.text: Use a Warehouse shortcut as the writable T-SQL alias of every raw PDF.
options.why: A reference to a file does not create the relational table and transactional workload required.

explanation: Choose engines from the required operations. A shared storage foundation does not make every item a file store or every endpoint writable.

title: Review a platform migration
prompt: A migration proposal places silver data in Warehouse and gold data in Lakehouse, then assumes existing SQL Server triggers will work unchanged. Select TWO appropriate review decisions.

options.text: Reject the proposal solely because gold cannot reside in Lakehouse.
options.why: Medallion labels describe data readiness, not a mandatory product assignment.

options.text: Approve every SQL Server object because the connection uses TDS.
options.why: Protocol compatibility does not imply complete SQL Server feature compatibility.

options.text: Evaluate supported T-SQL features and redesign unsupported trigger-based logic.
options.why: Warehouse has a documented SQL subset; trigger-based migration needs an alternative.

options.text: Judge the silver/gold placement using the actual processing and consumption requirements.
options.why: The item choice should follow operations and workload ownership, not color names.

explanation: The proposed stage placement can be reasonable. Independently review the SQL surface before committing to a migration.

title: Design a recurring load
prompt: Every night, eight source tables must be copied into Warehouse. A SQL validation procedure must run only after all eight copies succeed. Business users also own one Power Query transformation that outputs a ninth table. Which design most directly meets these requirements?

options.text: Schedule nine independent jobs and schedule the procedure at a fixed later time.
options.why: Elapsed time does not establish that every required load succeeded.

options.text: Use a view to combine the tables and rely on query execution to orchestrate loads.
options.why: A read view does not establish ingestion success dependencies.

options.text: Use one Copy Job and require users to check the ninth table manually.
options.why: That omits the explicit transformation and coordinated downstream success condition.

options.text: Orchestrate the copies and the Dataflow Gen2 in a Pipeline, then run the SQL procedure on success dependencies.
options.why: The Pipeline coordinates completion, while Dataflow Gen2 retains the business-owned transformation.

explanation: Separate transformation ownership from orchestration. Successful completion, rather than a clock delay, gates validation.

title: Choose a notebook execution surface
prompt: A notebook contains documented T-SQL steps that create and populate Warehouse tables. A Lakehouse SQL endpoint is currently its primary data source; a Warehouse is also attached. Unqualified writes fail. Which change addresses the execution context without translating the logic into Spark?

options.text: Set the Warehouse as the primary T-SQL notebook data source, and qualify cross-database references explicitly.
options.why: The primary source determines where unqualified T-SQL runs; Warehouse supports the target writes.

options.text: Attach the Warehouse again and leave the Lakehouse endpoint as primary.
options.why: Attaching a source alone does not redirect the unqualified write context.

options.text: Grant INSERT on the Lakehouse SQL endpoint table.
options.why: An additional grant cannot enable an unsupported underlying-data write operation.

options.text: Prefix the statement with an ABFSS path instead of a SQL database name.
options.why: A storage URI is not the SQL execution context or a three-part SQL identifier.

explanation: A notebook is an authoring surface. Its selected SQL execution target still controls what statements can run.

title: Assess a Spark loading proposal
prompt: An engineer proposes using the native Spark Warehouse connector to write a transformed DataFrame. The notebook runs on an older runtime, and a service principal is expected to authenticate through that connector. Select TWO issues to resolve under the documented connector contract.

options.text: The target must be Lakehouse because the connector is read-only in every runtime.
options.why: Current connector documentation includes Warehouse writes on the required runtime.

options.text: The connector supports interactive Entra user authentication, not service principal authentication.
options.why: A supported TDS service principal connection does not imply support in this native Spark connector.

options.text: Use the documented Runtime 2.0 write capability or select a different supported loading path.
options.why: The current connector write capability is runtime-dependent.

options.text: Disable Warehouse security so the connector can write directly to Parquet files.
options.why: Bypassing the supported connector and permissions is not a runtime or authentication fix.

explanation: Check the connector separately from the Warehouse engine. Authentication and runtime support are specific to the client path.

title: Migrate an external SQL client
prompt: A reporting application uses a SQL username/password and enables MultipleActiveResultSets. The administrator replaces only the server name with the Fabric Warehouse SQL connection string. The application still fails. Select TWO client changes appropriate to the documented interface.

options.text: Use an Entra-capable driver and a supported Entra authentication mode with authorized identity access.
options.why: The Fabric SQL interface supports Entra principals; the old SQL-authentication configuration is insufficient.

options.text: Keep SQL authentication and use the OneLake HTTPS endpoint instead.
options.why: A storage endpoint does not provide an alternative SQL username/password service.

options.text: Use an ABFSS URL as Initial Catalog.
options.why: Initial Catalog identifies a SQL database, not a file-system storage path.

options.text: Remove MultipleActiveResultSets or set it to false.
options.why: MARS is not supported on this Warehouse connection.

explanation: A compatible SQL wire protocol still has authentication and driver constraints. Check network reachability and permissions after fixing these client settings.

title: Investigate cross-item access
prompt: An analyst obtains a Warehouse SQL server name from settings and sees a second item's name in a query example. The analyst has Read item permission and SELECT on one Warehouse table only. A query of the second item's protected table fails. Which conclusion is warranted?

options.text: The SQL server name automatically grants SELECT on all items in its workspace.
options.why: An endpoint identifier does not expand the principal's authorized data access.

options.text: Adding the second item to Object Explorer grants access to its rows.
options.why: An editor attachment is a discovery convenience, not a SQL permission grant.

options.text: Verify the second item's access and object permissions for the executing identity.
options.why: The client can address a table and still lack authorization to read it.

options.text: Switch from SSMS to the visual query editor to bypass the object permissions.
options.why: Changing the query-authoring interface does not bypass the engine's authorization.

explanation: Distinguish connection, object discovery, and row access. A usable connection string does not grant blanket access.

title: Select reusable SQL objects
prompt: Finance requires an always-current reusable SELECT over employee rows, a scalar calculation returning one fiscal-quarter label, and an executable operation that performs approved updates. Which object assignment best fits?

options.text: Table for the current SELECT, view for the scalar calculation, function for the updates.
options.why: This substitutes stored rows for a reusable query and assigns writes to the wrong abstraction.

options.text: View for the reusable SELECT, scalar function for the label, stored procedure for the update operation.
options.why: These separate read-query reuse, a returned scalar value, and an executable write workflow.

options.text: Stored procedure for all three because views and functions cannot be queried in Warehouse.
options.why: Warehouse supports views and functions; a single procedure is not required for all three needs.

options.text: Schema for the SELECT, table constraint for the scalar label, shortcut for the updates.
options.why: Those organize names, describe constraints, or reference data rather than implement these operations.

explanation: Choose an object by its contract, not just its ability to contain SQL text. Schemas organize the resulting objects.

title: Validate a visual join
prompt: A visual query joins three employees to Addresses by EmployeeID. Employee 1 has two addresses, employee 2 has one, and employee 3 has none. Finance needs exactly one row per employee, retaining employees with no address. The developer selects an inner join and adds DISTINCT. What should be changed?

options.text: Keep the inner join; DISTINCT restores missing employees.
options.why: DISTINCT removes duplicate projected rows but cannot recreate unmatched employees.

options.text: Change only to a left join; it guarantees one row per employee.
options.why: A left join retains unmatched rows but still multiplies employees with multiple addresses.

options.text: Add a current timestamp column before DISTINCT to choose the latest address.
options.why: A query timestamp neither ranks the addresses nor selects a single child row.

options.text: Use a left join to a deterministically selected one-address-per-employee result.
options.why: Control child-table grain before joining, then retain unmatched parent employees.

explanation: The visual editor generates SQL; it does not certify the business grain. The required result has three rows, with a null address for employee 3.

title: Evaluate employee tenure
prompt: A view marks employees Senior when DATEDIFF(year, HireDate, @AsOfDate) >= 5. For this test, @AsOfDate is 2026-01-01 and HireDate is 2021-12-31. The policy requires five completed hire-date anniversaries. Which outcome and change are correct?

options.text: The expression returns 5 and incorrectly marks the employee Senior; compare the fifth anniversary to @AsOfDate.
options.why: Five year boundaries were crossed, but the fifth anniversary is 2026-12-31 and has not occurred.

options.text: The expression returns 4 and already enforces completed anniversaries.
options.why: DATEDIFF counts datepart boundaries, not completed years of tenure.

options.text: The expression returns 5; divide elapsed days by 365 to enforce exact anniversaries.
options.why: A fixed-day division is not exact anniversary logic across varying calendar years.

options.text: The expression returns NULL because the view uses a date parameter.
options.why: The supplied dates are valid values; the issue is boundary-count semantics.

explanation: For the non-leap-day dates given, test DATEADD(year, 5, HireDate) <= @AsOfDate. Define a separate business policy for leap-day hires.

title: Repair an optional filter
prompt: The procedure must always restrict Seniority to @Level. When @DepartmentID is NULL it must include every department, including employees whose DepartmentID is NULL. Otherwise it must match that department. Which predicate meets the contract?

options.text: WHERE Seniority = @Level OR DepartmentID = @DepartmentID
options.why: OR allows nonmatching seniority rows whenever the department matches.

options.text: WHERE Seniority = @Level AND DepartmentID = COALESCE(@DepartmentID, DepartmentID)
options.why: With a null parameter, a null department compares to NULL and evaluates UNKNOWN, excluding that employee.

options.text: WHERE Seniority = @Level AND (@DepartmentID IS NULL OR DepartmentID = @DepartmentID)
options.why: The null-parameter branch is true for all departments, while the outer AND preserves the seniority filter.

options.text: WHERE Seniority = @Level AND (@DepartmentID = NULL OR DepartmentID = @DepartmentID)
options.why: Equality to NULL is not a null test; it evaluates UNKNOWN and does not implement the optional branch.

explanation: Parentheses preserve the intended logical grouping. IS NULL implements the optional parameter without silently excluding null-valued departments.

title: Predict procedure output
prompt: A Warehouse table has four rows: (1, Senior, 10), (2, Junior, 10), (3, Senior, NULL), (4, Senior, 20). The repaired predicate from the code below is used. Which employee IDs are returned for @Level='Senior' with @DepartmentID=NULL, and then with @DepartmentID=10?

options.text: NULL parameter: 1,4. Department 10: 1,2.
options.why: This both loses the null-department Senior and admits the Junior in department 10.

options.text: NULL parameter: 1,3,4. Department 10: 1.
options.why: The optional department condition admits all Senior rows when null, and only Senior department 10 otherwise.

options.text: NULL parameter: none. Department 10: 1.
options.why: IS NULL makes the optional branch true; it is not an equality-to-null comparison.

options.text: NULL parameter: 1,2,3,4. Department 10: 1,2.
options.why: Seniority remains mandatory in both executions.

explanation: Evaluate the mandatory filter first, then the optional department branch. The null parameter means no department restriction, not only null-valued departments.
code:
WHERE Seniority = @Level
  AND (@DepartmentID IS NULL OR DepartmentID = @DepartmentID)

title: Reuse a parameterized result
prompt: A reporting query needs to join a reusable parameterized SELECT to Department without first executing a write workflow. An existing procedure returns that SELECT as a result set. Which redesign best meets the composable read requirement?

options.text: SELECT * FROM dbo.ExistingProcedure(@DepartmentID) JOIN Department ...
options.why: A stored procedure execution is not a table expression that can be used this way in FROM.

options.text: Put the procedure call inside a view and assume its parameters are passed by the view.
options.why: A view is not a parameterized procedure wrapper with that execution contract.

options.text: Convert the operation to a schema so it can be joined by its name.
options.why: A schema is a namespace, not a parameterized row-returning expression.

options.text: Use a supported inline table-valued function for the read logic, then join its returned rows.
options.why: An inline TVF provides a parameterized relational result composable in a SELECT.

explanation: Keep stored procedures for executable workflows. A composable parameterized read needs a relational expression such as an inline TVF.

title: Review a saved reporting query
prompt: A developer saves a visual query as a view and uses Copilot to add a LEFT JOIN plus a filter on the right table in WHERE. No physical reporting table was requested. Select TWO necessary review conclusions.

options.text: The saved view represents query logic; saving it does not materialize an independent copy of its result rows.
options.why: A ordinary view evaluates its definition over source data rather than acting as an independent loaded table.

options.text: Because the query was generated visually, row grain and filter behavior are already validated.
options.why: Generated SQL still needs review against the business requirements and representative data.

options.text: Check whether the WHERE predicate removes null-extended rows and defeats the required outer-join behavior.
options.why: A right-side predicate can reject unmatched rows; placement and null handling affect the result.

options.text: Treat Copilot output as proof that the query works on every Fabric SQL surface.
options.why: Assisted authoring does not establish correctness or support on the selected endpoint.

explanation: Saving and assisted authoring do not remove semantic review. Test unmatched rows and cardinality before adopting a reporting definition.

title: Diagnose source authorization
prompt: COPY INTO runs against a private Azure Blob CSV with no CREDENTIAL clause and no ERRORFILE option. The executing Entra user has the required Fabric connection access, INSERT, and ADMINISTER DATABASE BULK OPERATIONS, but only Azure management-plane Reader on the storage account. Source access fails. Which least-privilege fix fits this case?

options.text: Grant Storage Blob Data Reader to the executing identity at the required source scope.
options.why: The default credential uses that Entra identity for source access; blob read is a data-plane permission.

options.text: Grant SELECT on the Warehouse target table instead of blob source access.
options.why: Warehouse SELECT does not authorize reading the external source bytes.

options.text: Use an anonymous source URL because omitting CREDENTIAL always means anonymous access.
options.why: For Fabric the executing user's Entra identity is the default source credential.

options.text: Grant Azure management-plane Contributor and assume it directly grants every blob read.
options.why: Management-plane roles are distinct from the blob data-plane authorization required here.

explanation: The target SQL permissions have already been supplied. Diagnose the independent source data authorization instead of adding unrelated Warehouse grants.

title: Separate source and target identities
prompt: A Warehouse has a configured Workspace Identity with Storage Blob Data Reader on the private source container. A human user has Viewer workspace access and INSERT on the target table, but no source data access. They use COPY INTO with CREDENTIAL=(IDENTITY='Workspace Identity'). Under the documented contract, which statement is correct?

options.text: The workspace identity becomes the SQL execution user for target authorization and audit attribution.
options.why: The statement remains in the executing user's SQL security context.

options.text: The human must also be granted direct blob source read access for this credential mode.
options.why: Workspace Identity is impersonated for source access; the human need not directly read that source.

options.text: Source access uses Workspace Identity, while target SQL permissions and audit attribution remain with the human.
options.why: This intentionally separates source authorization from the statement's SQL execution identity.

options.text: INSERT is unnecessary because source read permission also grants target write permission.
options.why: Source authorization does not grant INSERT into the Warehouse target.

explanation: This is a current-source extension to the video's default-user COPY example. With Workspace Identity, the documented INSERT requirement remains; ADMINISTER DATABASE BULK OPERATIONS is not required in this mode.

title: Configure a headered CSV load
prompt: An existing Warehouse target has columns EmployeeID, Name, Salary in that order. A UTF-8 CSV has the same column order, a single header line, and comma-delimited data. The source and SQL permissions are correct. Which configuration loads the data rows without treating the header as employee data?

options.text: FILE_TYPE='PARQUET', FIRSTROW=2
options.why: The file is CSV; the selected parser must match its actual format.

options.text: FILE_TYPE='CSV', FIRSTROW=2
options.why: CSV parsing plus skipping the single header fits the stated layout.

options.text: FILE_TYPE='CSV', FIRSTROW=1
options.why: This begins with the header rather than skipping it.

options.text: FILE_TYPE='CSV', FIRSTROW=3
options.why: This skips the header and the first actual employee row.

explanation: Format and row-offset settings are independent of access permissions. This is an original code exercise, not a reconstruction of unseen on-screen SQL.

title: Make a retry safe
prompt: An append-only COPY INTO loads three new employees into a six-row target. The operation succeeds, but the orchestrator loses the success response and retries the same file. The target has no enforced uniqueness or deduplication logic. Which design best prevents duplicates on a replay?

options.text: Add a NOT ENFORCED primary key and assume the engine rejects repeated EmployeeIDs.
options.why: A declared unenforced constraint does not implement duplicate rejection.

options.text: Change FIRSTROW to 2 on the retry because it skips already-loaded employees.
options.why: FIRSTROW skips file rows such as the header, not rows already present in the target.

options.text: Create a view with DISTINCT and keep appending indefinitely.
options.why: A view can hide some repeated projected rows but leaves the target load non-idempotent.

options.text: Stage the batch, validate a deterministic business key, and apply an idempotent key-based load with batch tracking.
options.why: Explicit replay handling protects the target; it does not rely on COPY to infer prior successful batches.

explanation: Under the stated append behavior, two successful executions produce 12 rows, not 9. Prevent replay duplication as part of the loading design.

title: Specify a reporting timestamp
prompt: A Warehouse report must read Orders and Customers as they existed at 2026-10-01 21:30 UTC. Both tables have retained history and unchanged schemas. A colleague converts that time to 23:30 local time and places separate AS OF clauses on each table. Which replacement is appropriate?

options.text: Use one SELECT-level OPTION (FOR TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-10-01T21:30:00').
options.why: The UTC timestamp and statement-level hint apply consistently to joined Warehouse tables.

options.text: Use one SELECT-level hint at 23:30 because the query uses the analyst's local time zone.
options.why: The documented time-travel timestamp is UTC, not the analyst's local-time display.

options.text: Set a different timestamp on each table within this SELECT's OPTION clause.
options.why: The hint is specified once for the statement, not independently per joined table.

options.text: Use the current view result because time travel changes only the query label.
options.why: The hint selects retained historical table data, not merely a display label.

explanation: Use a single shared business cutoff expressed in UTC. The statement-level hint makes this a stable historical read.

title: Assess an audit query
prompt: An auditor needs to SELECT a historical Warehouse table state from ten days ago. The Warehouse still retains that state. Current security restricts the auditor to their region. Select TWO correct expectations.

options.text: Historical queries bypass current RLS because the rows existed before the auditor's grant.
options.why: Time travel does not remove the security restrictions imposed when the auditor queries.

options.text: The result is read-only under the FOR TIMESTAMP AS OF hint.
options.why: The historical-query hint is for SELECT, not direct INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE of the snapshot.

options.text: Current query security restrictions remain applicable to the auditor's historical read.
options.why: Historical access is still governed, including applicable RLS, CLS, and masking.

options.text: The auditor can UPDATE the past state by adding the same OPTION to an UPDATE statement.
options.why: The hint is not a write-to-the-past operation.

explanation: A historical snapshot is a governed read. It is not an alternative route to mutate data or evade current authorization.

title: Reassess a retention requirement
prompt: A production Warehouse must support queries of retained states up to 60 calendar days old going forward. A runbook copied from the 2025 video says the 30-day retention is fixed. Which current-source correction is appropriate?

options.text: Keep the fixed 30-day limit and use OPTIMIZE to recover the missing history.
options.why: Compaction does not extend the historical retention window.

options.text: Use a Lakehouse VACUUM setting to change the Warehouse's retention.
options.why: Lakehouse table cleanup settings do not configure the Warehouse policy.

options.text: Pause capacity for 30 days so retained versions stop aging.
options.why: Version age is measured in calendar days, including paused-capacity time.

options.text: Configure the Warehouse retention to 60 whole days and verify actual available history.
options.why: Current Warehouse retention is configurable from 1 to 120 days; a setting does not recreate old deleted history.

explanation: The video accurately reflects an older contract. Configure the policy ahead of need and distinguish its future window from data currently recoverable.

title: Investigate a missing historical state
prompt: Warehouse retention was seven days. Garbage collection already removed the state from 20 days ago. Today the administrator increases retention to 60 days, then requests that 20-day-old state. Which outcome is justified?

options.text: The request succeeds because ALTER DATABASE recreates prior Parquet versions.
options.why: Changing retention cannot recreate historical data that has already been removed.

options.text: The deleted state remains unavailable; inspect the actual retention cutoff instead of assuming a full 60-day history.
options.why: The new policy preserves available and future history, not previously cleaned-up versions.

options.text: The state becomes available after the next OPTIMIZE run.
options.why: An active-data optimization does not reconstruct deleted prior states.

options.text: The state returns if capacity is paused and resumed.
options.why: Capacity lifecycle does not restore cleaned-up historical files.

explanation: Increasing a retention setting cannot undo completed cleanup. The actual recoverable-history cutoff can differ from the configured window.

title: Review schema history
prompt: Yesterday dbo.Employee had EmployeeID and Salary. Today a nullable Bonus column was added. The earlier data remains retained. A SELECT requests EmployeeID, Bonus at yesterday's timestamp. Which diagnosis fits the current contract?

options.text: Every earlier data row is lost whenever any nullable column is added.
options.why: A query of columns that already existed can still access the retained earlier state.

options.text: Time travel automatically recreates yesterday's complete table definition and invents Bonus as NULL.
options.why: The current schema is used; selecting a column introduced after the requested time is unsupported.

options.text: The request fails because Bonus did not exist then; a historical query of EmployeeID can still succeed.
options.why: Separate historical data availability from the selected columns' schema availability.

options.text: Replacing Bonus with SELECT * guarantees a historical schema reconstruction.
options.why: Selecting all current columns does not remove the newly introduced column problem.

explanation: The time-travel query returns historical data through the current schema constraints. Dropping and recreating a table also removes that table's history.

title: Compare Warehouse and Lakehouse history
prompt: An architect claims the Warehouse time-travel syntax can never apply to any Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint. Current documentation describes endpoint time travel as Preview. Which condition is necessary before relying on that endpoint feature?

options.text: The SQL analytics endpoint must have been created with New metadata sync enabled, and the needed table history must survive vacuum retention.
options.why: Current endpoint support is conditional and table history depends on the Lakehouse cleanup policy.

options.text: Set ALTER DATABASE Warehouse retention to 120 days on the endpoint.
options.why: The configurable Warehouse retention policy does not apply to a Lakehouse SQL endpoint.

options.text: Create any view and assume it creates missing Delta history.
options.why: A SQL view does not manufacture deleted historical table versions.

options.text: Run the time-travel hint through any Spark Warehouse connector query because all SQL syntax is supported there.
options.why: The native connector documents a time-travel-query limitation; engine support is not universal client support.

explanation: Treat the conditional Preview endpoint capability separately from Warehouse support. Verify creation settings, retained table data, and the client contract.

title: Materialize a curated copy
prompt: SalesWH and RawLH are in the same active workspace. RawLH has a synchronized, schema-enabled SQL table raw.Employee. Required permissions and compatible target types are present. Finance needs an independently stored Warehouse table populated from those rows. Which operation meets that requirement?

options.text: Create a Files shortcut and expect an independent Warehouse table to appear.
options.why: A file reference does not materialize the target relational rows.

options.text: CREATE VIEW SalesWH.dbo.Employee AS SELECT ... FROM RawLH.raw.Employee;
options.why: A view retains a query dependency and does not independently load the target data.

options.text: INSERT INTO RawLH.raw.Employee SELECT ... FROM SalesWH.dbo.Employee;
options.why: This reverses the requested direction and attempts underlying-data DML through a Lakehouse SQL endpoint.

options.text: INSERT INTO SalesWH.dbo.Employee (EmployeeID,Name) SELECT EmployeeID,Name FROM RawLH.raw.Employee;
options.why: An explicit column-mapped INSERT SELECT copies the authorized source rows into the Warehouse target.

explanation: A three-part name identifies database, schema, and table. The direction and target write capability determine whether the copy is supported.

title: Count a combined result
prompt: Warehouse table W has (1,'A') and (2,'B'). Lakehouse table L has (2,'B') and (3,'C'). The query below uses UNION, includes the literal Source column, and has no other rows. How many rows are returned, and what happens if Source is removed from both projections?

options.text: Four rows; three after removing Source.
options.why: The two employee-2 rows differ by Source in the first query; without Source they become duplicates removed by UNION.

options.text: Three rows in both queries because UNION deduplicates solely by EmployeeID.
options.why: UNION compares the full projected row, not an assumed business key.

options.text: Four rows in both queries because UNION never removes duplicates.
options.why: UNION without ALL removes duplicate projected rows.

options.text: Two rows first; four after removing Source.
options.why: Neither result follows the full-row duplicate semantics of UNION.

explanation: Provenance columns change row equality. UNION ALL would preserve four input rows in either projection; choose deduplication at the intended business grain.

title: Assess workspace scope
prompt: Two Warehouses are in different workspaces. A developer wants to copy the same three-part-name query used in the video's same-workspace demo, merely adding the other item to Object Explorer. No shortcut or supported external-access design has been configured. Which review response is appropriate?

options.text: Approve it because three-part naming contains a hidden workspace component.
options.why: The three components identify database, schema, and object, not an arbitrary remote workspace route.

options.text: The demonstrated cross-database route is documented for the current workspace; design a supported cross-workspace access path separately.
options.why: Do not infer arbitrary cross-workspace SQL reachability from the same-workspace demo.

options.text: Use a four-part workspace name and assume it bypasses source permissions.
options.why: Inventing an identifier does not establish a supported cross-workspace route or authorization.

options.text: Convert the query to a visual query because canvas joins have no workspace boundary.
options.why: The visual authoring surface does not eliminate the underlying access contract.

explanation: Scope the demonstrated feature precisely. A source reference, a physical load, and a cross-workspace route are separate architecture decisions.

title: Predict recovery rows
prompt: At 09:00 source Employee has 11 rows and a clone is created. At 09:05 a twelfth source row is inserted. At 09:10 the source is truncated. At 09:15 the source is repopulated by INSERT SELECT from the clone. Schemas remain unchanged, permissions are present, and no other changes occur. Which final row counts are correct?

options.text: Source 12; clone 12.
options.why: The clone does not track the source's post-clone insert.

options.text: Source 0; clone 0.
options.why: Truncating the source does not propagate to the independent clone.

options.text: Source 11; clone 11.
options.why: Recovery copies the clone's 09:00 state; the later twelfth row is absent from it.

options.text: Source 12; clone 11.
options.why: The restore source contains only 11 rows, so it cannot reintroduce the twelfth row.

explanation: The narrated demonstration illustrates independent tables, not live synchronization. Recovery from an older clone can intentionally omit valid later changes.

title: Choose a testing branch
prompt: A tester needs an independently writable copy of a Warehouse table in a different schema of the same Warehouse. Initial duplication of the large data files must be avoided. The tester has the documented clone permissions and must not see future production updates automatically. Which choice meets the requirements?

options.text: A supported table clone into the test schema.
options.why: A zero-copy clone starts from shared files but presents an independent table state.

options.text: A Lakehouse shortcut to the production table.
options.why: A plain shortcut is a reference with a source dependency, not this independent Warehouse test branch.

options.text: A view over the production table.
options.why: The read query continues to evaluate the production source rather than creating the requested independent table.

options.text: INSERT SELECT into a new table because every clone duplicates all Parquet files immediately.
options.why: A clone copies metadata rather than initially duplicating the entire data-file set.

explanation: Zero-copy describes clone creation, not a promise of no future storage use. Source and clone can subsequently diverge.

title: Review isolation and protection
prompt: A team proposes cloning a sensitive Warehouse table into another schema of the same Warehouse. It expects production changes to stop propagating, but assumes the clone has no inherited SQL security. Select TWO accurate review conclusions.

options.text: The clone becomes a live alias of production until a full copy is explicitly requested.
options.why: A clone is independent from creation; it is not a live shortcut.

options.text: Source changes do not automatically change the clone's rows.
options.why: DML and DDL changes are independent after clone creation.

options.text: A clone never inherits masking or RLS, so every existing policy must be presumed absent.
options.why: Current clone documentation describes inheritance of these protections.

options.text: Review inherited object security, RLS, and masking, then validate the intended tester's effective access.
options.why: Inheritance exists, but effective visibility still depends on privileges and workspace roles.

explanation: The video's security-inheritance claim is supported. Inheritance is not equivalent to anonymization or assurance that a privileged tester sees only masked data.

title: Check clone placement
prompt: A Warehouse table must be cloned at a retained historical UTC timestamp. No schema changes have occurred. The proposal creates the clone in a second Warehouse in the same workspace. Which revision fits the current supported placement?

options.text: Keep the destination because sharing a workspace is sufficient for cross-Warehouse cloning.
options.why: The current clone limitation is narrower than the workspace boundary.

options.text: Create the table clone within the source Warehouse, optionally in a different schema, using the AT timestamp syntax.
options.why: Current and historical table clones are supported within one Warehouse, including across its schemas.

options.text: Run CREATE TABLE AS CLONE OF against the Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint instead.
options.why: Warehouse table cloning is not supported on that Lakehouse endpoint.

options.text: Use CLONE OF the whole schema and assume it clones every child table atomically.
options.why: The documented primitive is table cloning, not a schema or Warehouse clone.

explanation: A supported same-workspace cross-database SELECT does not imply cross-Warehouse clone support. Check both placement and retention before cloning.

title: Sequence a controlled recovery
prompt: A bad load has damaged a Warehouse employee table. Valid retained history from immediately before the load exists; the schema is unchanged. You must inspect a recoverable branch before changing production, and preserve a clear authorization checkpoint. Arrange the steps.

options.text: Validate row counts, keys, and critical totals on the recovery branch.
options.why: Validation determines whether the candidate state satisfies the business recovery requirements.

options.text: Identify the correct pre-load UTC timestamp and verify available history and clone permissions.
options.why: Choose and authorize the recovery state before creating a candidate branch.

options.text: After approval, apply the controlled recovery to production and verify the resulting data.
options.why: The production change follows validation and the approval checkpoint; verify the completed recovery.

options.text: Create a same-Warehouse historical table clone at that timestamp as a recovery candidate.
options.why: A separate candidate supports inspection before production is changed.

explanation: Time travel identifies a state; a clone provides an inspectable branch. This workflow does not assume that every valid change after the selected timestamp should be discarded.
